title: Steps in the Community Mobilisation Process
path: Steps in the Community Mobilisation Process

headings.title: Introduction to Community Mobilisation
headings.content: Community mobilisation is a capacity-building process that brings people, groups, and organizations together to plan, carry out, and evaluate activities on a participatory and sustained basis. In the Nigerian Primary Health Care context, this process empowers local populations to take charge of their own health outcomes rather than remaining passive recipients of medical services. Nurses working at the primary health care level often act as catalysts or facilitators. Success depends heavily on respecting local culture, traditions, and existing power structures.

headings.title: Entry and Community Profiling
headings.content:
The first official step involves entering the community and building initial rapport. Before conducting any health intervention, the health worker must officially greet community gatekeepers, such as traditional rulers, local government chairmen, and religious leaders. Community profiling follows this entry phase, involving data collection on population size, dominant occupations, prevailing health issues, geographical boundaries, and existing infrastructure. 

- **Gatekeeper Engagement**: Gaining official entry and permission to work in the area.
- **Demographic Mapping**: Identifying age distribution, vulnerable groups, and settlement patterns.
- **Resource Inventory**: Noting available health facilities, schools, and water sources.

headings.title: Sensitization and Awareness Creation
headings.content: Once the community profile is clear, the focus shifts to sensitization. This step breaks down resistance and builds curiosity and desire for health improvement. Nurses utilize town criers, church and mosque announcements, community meetings, and local drama groups to pass messages. The goal is to ensure that everyone understands the purpose of the upcoming health programs and recognizes their personal stake in the outcomes.

headings.title: Identifying and Training Stakeholders
headings.content: Sustainable health initiatives require local champions. During this step, the nurse identifies influential individuals, youth leaders, women's group heads, and traditional birth attendants who can drive the process. These stakeholders undergo specialized training to equip them with basic health knowledge, communication skills, and leadership techniques, transforming them into community-based health volunteers.

headings.title: Needs Assessment and Priority Setting
headings.content: Communities often face multiple challenges, but health workers cannot solve everything at once. Needs assessment involves participatory tools like focus group discussions and interviews to discover what the community actually views as its greatest burden. Once needs are listed, the community collaborates with nurses to rank them in order of urgency, feasibility, and impact, ensuring that limited resources target the most pressing health threat.

headings.title: Action Planning and Resource Mobilisation
headings.content: With priorities set, stakeholders draft a concrete action plan detailing who will do what, when, and with what resources. Resource mobilisation follows immediately, tapping into local assets such as communal labor, vacant buildings, financial contributions, and external donations. Relying purely on external funding creates dependency, so local contributions remain critical for long-term project survival.

headings.title: Implementation of Health Interventions
headings.content: Action plans transform into reality during the implementation phase. Nurses collaborate directly with trained volunteers and community members to execute activities such as immunization drives, sanitation campaigns, or health education workshops. Active participation during this stage ensures that services reach target populations effectively and cultural barriers are managed smoothly on the ground.

headings.title: Monitoring, Evaluation, and Sustainability
headings.content: The final stage determines if the objectives were met and ensures the program can continue without constant outside supervision. Monitoring occurs continuously to catch challenges early, while evaluation assesses overall impact. Sustainability is achieved when the community takes full ownership, maintains facilities, and continues health practices independently.
